usamo-usamo-1975-01.title: Fractional parts, then Legendre's formula
usamo-usamo-1975-01.body:
**Lemma.** For all real $x, y\ge 0$:
$$[5x]+[5y] \ge [x]+[y]+[3x+y]+[3y+x]. \tag{L}$$

*Reduction.* Write $x = i + \alpha$, $y = j + \beta$ with integers $i,j\ge0$ and $\alpha,\beta\in[0,1)$. Since $[z + k] = [z] + k$ for integers $k$, both sides of (L) increase by exactly $5i+5j$ when passing from $(\alpha,\beta)$ to $(x,y)$ (the right side by $(i+j) + (3i+j) + (3j+i)$). So it suffices to prove (L) for $0\le x,y<1$, where $[x]=[y]=0$.

*Case check.* Let $A = [5x]$, $B = [5y]$, so $A, B\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ and $x<\frac{A+1}5$, $y<\frac{B+1}5$. Then $3x+y < \frac{3A+B+4}{5}$. If an integer $N$ satisfies $N \le z < \frac{M}{5}$ for an integer $M$, then $5N < M$, so $5N\le M-1$; hence
$$[3x+y] \le \Big\lfloor \tfrac{3A+B+3}{5}\Big\rfloor,\qquad [3y+x] \le \Big\lfloor \tfrac{A+3B+3}{5}\Big\rfloor.$$
Call the sum of these bounds $S(A,B)$; it is symmetric, so take $A\le B$. If $A + B\ge 6$ then $S \le \frac{4A+4B+6}{5} \le A+B$. The remaining cases:

| $(A,B)$ | (0,0) | (0,1) | (0,2) | (0,3) | (0,4) | (1,1) | (1,2) | (1,3) | (1,4) | (2,2) | (2,3) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $S$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 5 | 4 | 4 |
| $A+B$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 4 | 5 |

In every case $S \le A + B$, so $[3x+y]+[3y+x] \le S \le [5x]+[5y]$. This proves (L), and (a) follows because $[x]+[y]\ge 0$.

**(b)** By Legendre's formula, the exponent of a prime $p$ in $N!$ is $\sum_{k\ge1}\left[N/p^k\right]$. So the exponent of $p$ in the given fraction is
$$\sum_{k\ge 1}\left( \Big[\tfrac{5m}{p^k}\Big] + \Big[\tfrac{5n}{p^k}\Big] - \Big[\tfrac{m}{p^k}\Big] - \Big[\tfrac{n}{p^k}\Big] - \Big[\tfrac{3m+n}{p^k}\Big] - \Big[\tfrac{3n+m}{p^k}\Big]\right).$$
Each summand is $\ge 0$ by (L) with $x = m/p^k$, $y = n/p^k$. Since every prime appears with non-negative exponent, the fraction is an integer. ∎

usamo-usamo-1975-02.title: Expand with vectors
usamo-usamo-1975-02.body:
Let $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$ be the position vectors of $A,B,C,D$, and use $|\vec u-\vec v|^2 = |\vec u|^2+|\vec v|^2 - 2\,\vec u\cdot\vec v$.

On the left, each of $|\vec a|^2, |\vec b|^2, |\vec c|^2, |\vec d|^2$ appears twice (e.g. $\vec a$ in $AC$ and $AD$); on the right each appears once. So
$$AC^2+BD^2+AD^2+BC^2-AB^2-CD^2$$
$$= |\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2+|\vec c|^2+|\vec d|^2 - 2(\vec a\cdot\vec c+\vec b\cdot\vec d+\vec a\cdot\vec d+\vec b\cdot\vec c) + 2(\vec a\cdot\vec b+\vec c\cdot\vec d)$$
$$= |\vec a+\vec b-\vec c-\vec d|^2 \;\ge\; 0,$$
as one sees by expanding the square. Equality holds iff $\vec a+\vec b = \vec c+\vec d$, i.e. iff segments $AB$ and $CD$ have the same midpoint. ∎

usamo-usamo-1975-02.title: Use the median formula
usamo-usamo-1975-02.body:
Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $AB$ and $CD$. By the median-length formula (Apollonius) in triangles $ABC$ and $ABD$,
$$AC^2 + BC^2 = 2CM^2 + \tfrac12 AB^2,\qquad AD^2+BD^2 = 2DM^2 + \tfrac12 AB^2.$$
Adding, and applying the same formula in triangle $CMD$ (with $N$ the midpoint of $CD$): $CM^2 + DM^2 = 2MN^2 + \tfrac12 CD^2$. So
$$AC^2+BD^2+AD^2+BC^2 = AB^2 + 4MN^2 + CD^2 \ge AB^2+CD^2. $$
∎

usamo-usamo-1975-03.title: Multiply out the denominator
usamo-usamo-1975-03.body:
Let $Q(x) = (x+1)P(x) - x$, a polynomial of degree at most $n+1$. For $k = 0,1,\dots,n$, $Q(k) = (k+1)\frac{k}{k+1} - k = 0$, so $Q$ has the $n+1$ roots $0, 1, \dots, n$ and therefore
$$Q(x) = c\,x(x-1)(x-2)\cdots(x-n)$$
for a constant $c$. Setting $x = -1$: $Q(-1) = 0 - (-1) = 1$, while the right side is $c\,(-1)(-2)\cdots(-(n+1)) = c\,(-1)^{n+1}(n+1)!$. So $c = \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}$.

Now set $x = n+1$:
$$(n+2)P(n+1) - (n+1) = c\,(n+1)! = (-1)^{n+1},$$
so
$$P(n+1) = \frac{n+1+(-1)^{n+1}}{n+2} = \begin{cases} 1, & n \text{ odd},\\[2pt] \dfrac{n}{n+2}, & n\text{ even}.\end{cases}$$
(Check $n=1$: $P(x) = x/2$, so $P(2) = 1$ ✓.)

usamo-usamo-1975-04.title: Chord lengths as projections
usamo-usamo-1975-04.body:
Let the circles have centers $O_1, O_2$ and radii $r_1, r_2$, and let $\vec u_1, \vec u_2$ be the unit vectors from $P$ towards $O_1, O_2$. Let $\varphi = \angle O_1PO_2$; since the circles meet in two points, $O_1, P, O_2$ are not collinear, so $0<\varphi<\pi$.

**Chord through $P$.** For a unit vector $\vec e$, the line $P + t\vec e$ meets circle 1 where $|P + t\vec e - O_1|^2 = r_1^2$, i.e. $t^2 - 2t\,r_1(\vec e\cdot\vec u_1) = 0$ (using $|P - O_1| = r_1$). So its second intersection is at $t = 2r_1(\vec e\cdot\vec u_1)$, and similarly at $t = 2r_2(\vec e\cdot\vec u_2)$ on circle 2. A segment $AB$ through $P$ with $A$ on circle 1 and $B$ on circle 2 needs these two values of $t$ to have opposite signs, and then
$$AP\cdot PB = 4r_1r_2\,\big|(\vec e\cdot\vec u_1)(\vec e\cdot\vec u_2)\big| = -4r_1r_2\,(\vec e\cdot\vec u_1)(\vec e\cdot\vec u_2).$$

**Optimization.** Measure the direction of $\vec e$ by its angle $\theta$ from the bisector of $\angle O_1PO_2$. Then $\vec e\cdot\vec u_1 = \cos(\theta - \varphi/2)$ and $\vec e\cdot\vec u_2 = \cos(\theta+\varphi/2)$, so
$$-(\vec e\cdot\vec u_1)(\vec e\cdot\vec u_2) = -\tfrac12\big(\cos 2\theta + \cos\varphi\big) \le \tfrac12(1 - \cos\varphi) = \sin^2\tfrac{\varphi}{2},$$
with equality iff $\cos 2\theta = -1$, i.e. $\theta = 90^\circ$. For this direction the product $(\vec e\cdot\vec u_1)(\vec e\cdot\vec u_2) = -\sin^2\frac\varphi2 < 0$, so $A$ and $B$ really are on opposite sides of $P$. Hence the maximum is
$$AP\cdot PB = 4r_1r_2\sin^2\tfrac{\varphi}{2},$$
attained exactly when $AB$ is perpendicular to the bisector of $\angle O_1PO_2$ (equivalently, $AB$ makes equal angles with $PO_1$ and $PO_2$; it is the external bisector of $\angle O_1PO_2$).

**Construction.** Join $P$ to the centers $O_1, O_2$. On ray $PO_2$ mark $H$ with $PH = PO_1$. Then $O_1H$ is perpendicular to the bisector of $\angle O_1PO_2$ (triangle $O_1PH$ is isosceles). Draw through $P$ the line parallel to $O_1H$; it meets the two circles again at the required $A$ and $B$.

usamo-usamo-1975-05.title: Reverse the deck
usamo-usamo-1975-05.body:
The number of cards turned up equals the position $J$ (from the top) of the second ace. The set of the three ace positions $\{i<j<k\}$ is a uniformly random $3$-element subset of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, since all orderings of the deck are equally likely.

Consider the map $t\mapsto n+1-t$ on positions (turning the deck upside down). It sends a $3$-subset $\{i<j<k\}$ to the $3$-subset $\{n+1-k < n+1-j < n+1-i\}$, and it is a bijection on $3$-subsets. The middle element of the image is $n+1-j$. Because the distribution of the subset is uniform, it is unchanged by this bijection, so $J$ and $n+1-J$ have the same distribution. Hence
$$E[J] = E[n+1-J] = n+1 - E[J],\qquad\text{so}\qquad E[J] = \frac{n+1}{2}.$$
∎

usamo-usamo-1975-05.title: Direct computation
usamo-usamo-1975-05.body:
The second ace is at position $j$ iff one ace is among positions $1,\dots,j-1$ and one among $j+1,\dots,n$, so $P(J=j) = \frac{(j-1)(n-j)}{\binom n3}$. Then
$$E[J] = \frac{1}{\binom n3}\sum_{j=1}^{n} j(j-1)(n-j).$$
Substituting $j \to n+1-j$ turns the sum into $\sum (n+1-j)(n-j)(j-1)$; adding the two forms gives $2\sum = (n+1)\sum_j (j-1)(n-j) = (n+1)\binom n3$ (the last sum counts the $3$-subsets by their middle element). So $E[J] = \frac{n+1}2$. ∎
